questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of physical quantities have the same dimensions?

solution.concept: Dimensions of mechanical quantities
solution.explanation: Work = force × displacement and torque = force × perpendicular distance. Both are a force multiplied by a length, so both have dimensions [M L² T⁻²], although torque is not a form of energy.
steps: Torque: [M L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²] → same
Force [M L T⁻²] vs pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]; power [M L² T⁻³] vs work [M L² T⁻²]; momentum [M L T⁻¹] vs kinetic energy [M L² T⁻²] → all different
solution.why_others_wrong: Pressure is force per unit area, power is work per unit time and kinetic energy has an extra factor of velocity compared with momentum, so each of these pairs differs in dimensions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensions of physical quantities

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (measured value) with List-II (number of significant figures in it).

List-I:
A. 0.00450
B. 6.0300
C. 20.05
D. 0.70

List-II:
I. 2
II. 3
III. 4
IV. 5

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rules for counting significant figures
solution.explanation: Leading zeros (zeros before the first non-zero digit) are not significant. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes either count the leading zeros of 0.00450, drop the trailing zero of 0.70, or drop the zeros sandwiched between 2 and 5 in 20.05.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The period of a pendulum is measured five times, giving 1.52 s, 1.48 s, 1.55 s, 1.45 s and 1.50 s. The mean absolute error of these measurements, rounded to two decimal places, is:

solution.concept: Mean value and mean absolute error
solution.explanation: The best estimate is the arithmetic mean of the readings. The absolute error of each reading is the magnitude of its difference from the mean, and the mean absolute error is the average of these magnitudes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.05 s is the largest single deviation, not the mean. 0.00 s averages the signed deviations, which always cancel. 0.14 s is the sum of the deviations, not divided by 5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', absolute error, relative error and percentage error

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Suppose force (F), velocity (v) and time (T) are chosen as the fundamental quantities instead of mass, length and time. The dimensional formula of mass in this system is:

solution.concept: Expressing a quantity in a new set of base quantities
solution.explanation: Write a physical relation that links mass with F, v and T. From Newton's second law, F = ma = m(v/T), so m = F T / v.
steps: F = m × (change in velocity)/(time) → F = m v / T
m = F T / v → [F v⁻¹ T]
solution.why_others_wrong: Check each in M, L, T: [F v T⁻¹] = [M L² T⁻⁴] (it inverts the relation), [F v⁻¹ T⁻¹] = [M T⁻²] and [F v⁻² T²] = [M L⁻¹ T²]. Only [F v⁻¹ T] reduces to [M].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional formulae and dimensional equations

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When two measured quantities are multiplied or divided, the maximum relative error in the result is the sum of the relative errors in the quantities.
Statement II: When one measured quantity is subtracted from another, the maximum absolute error in the result is the difference of their absolute errors.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Combination of errors
solution.explanation: For Z = AB or Z = A/B, ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B. For Z = A + B or Z = A − B, the maximum absolute error is ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB in both cases: errors always add in the worst case, even when the quantities are subtracted.
steps: Statement I: relative errors add for a product or a quotient → true
Statement II: for Z = A − B, ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB (not ΔA − ΔB) → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is the common trap: subtracting the quantities does not subtract their errors, because the errors can have either sign and the maximum error is their sum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a simple pendulum experiment, g is found from g = 4π²L/T². The length L is measured as 100.0 cm with a scale of least count 1 mm. The time taken for 20 oscillations is measured as 40 s with a watch of resolution 1 s. The maximum percentage error in the value of g is:

solution.concept: Percentage error from least counts, and the power rule
solution.explanation: The relative error in L is its least count divided by L. Timing 20 oscillations together means the 1 s resolution applies to the 40 s total, so ΔT/T = 1/40. Since g ∝ L T⁻², the relative error in g is ΔL/L + 2 ΔT/T.
solution.shortcut: Timing N oscillations divides the timing error by N; that is why the experiment counts many.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.6% forgets the factor 2 from T². 5.0% ignores the error in L. 100.1% applies the 1 s resolution to a single period of 2 s instead of to the 40 s total.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) A dimensionally correct equation need not be a correct physical relation.
(b) An equation that is dimensionally inconsistent must be wrong.
(c) Dimensional analysis gives the values of the dimensionless constants in a physical relation.
(d) In a number written without a decimal point, the trailing zeros are not significant.
(e) The number of significant figures in a measured value depends on the unit in which it is expressed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Uses and limits of dimensional analysis; significant figures
solution.explanation: Dimensional consistency is necessary but not sufficient for a relation to be correct. Dimensional analysis cannot find pure numbers such as 1/2 or 2π. By NCERT's rules, trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are not significant, and a change of units does not change the number of significant figures.
steps: (a) True: e.g. s = ut + at² is dimensionally correct but wrong (the factor 1/2 is missing)
(b) True: terms of different dimensions cannot be equated
(c) False: dimensionless constants cannot be found by this method
(d) True: e.g. 123000 mm has three significant figures
(e) False: 2.308 cm = 0.02308 m = 23.08 mm, all with four significant figures
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with (c) or (e) includes a false statement; (a), (b) and (d) are all true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures and dimensional analysis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car moving along a straight road at 72 km/h is brought to rest with uniform retardation in 4 s. The distance it covers while stopping is:

solution.concept: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
solution.explanation: Convert the speed to m/s. With uniform retardation, the distance is the average velocity multiplied by the time.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 m multiplies the initial speed by the time, as if the speed stayed 20 m/s. 120 m adds ½at² instead of subtracting it (sign of the retardation). 144 m uses 72 without converting km/h to m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following CANNOT be the position–time graph of a particle moving along a straight line?

options.text: A straight line parallel to the time axis
A straight line inclined to the time axis
A curve that bends back so that it shows two different positions at the same instant of time
A parabola with its vertex on the position axis

solution.concept: Physical meaning of a position–time graph
solution.explanation: At any one instant a particle can be at only one position. A graph that gives two positions for the same time therefore cannot describe a real motion.
steps: Line parallel to the time axis → particle at rest
Two positions at one instant → impossible
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three graphs describe rest, uniform motion and uniformly accelerated motion, all of which are possible.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', position-time graphs
solution.final_answer: Option C: A curve that bends back so that it shows two different positions at the same instant of time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For the vectors A = 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ and B = î − ĵ + k̂, the scalar product A · B is:

solution.concept: Scalar product in component form
solution.explanation: A · B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z, keeping the sign of every component.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 takes (−1)(1) as +1. 6 adds the products without their signs. 4 takes 3 × (−1) as +3 and gets the k̂ term right.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the scalar product

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle moves along a circle of radius 0.5 m at a constant rate of 2 revolutions per second. The magnitude of its centripetal acceleration is:

solution.concept: Centripetal acceleration a = ω²r
solution.explanation: Convert the frequency to angular speed (ω = 2πν) and use a = ω²r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2π is the speed v = ωr in m/s, not the acceleration. 2 m/s² uses ω = 2 rad/s, mistaking rev/s for rad/s. 32π² m/s² divides by r instead of multiplying.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', uniform circular motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two trains, 100 m and 150 m long, move on parallel tracks in opposite directions with speeds of 20 m/s and 30 m/s. The time they take to cross each other completely is:

solution.concept: Relative velocity in one dimension
solution.explanation: In the frame of one train, the other approaches with the relative speed 20 + 30 = 50 m/s and must cover the sum of the two lengths before they have fully passed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 s uses the difference of speeds (trains moving the same way). 3 s and 2 s use the length of only one train.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', relative velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A projectile is launched from level ground, and its horizontal range turns out to be equal to the maximum height it reaches. Neglecting air resistance, the angle of projection above the horizontal is:

solution.concept: Range and maximum height of a projectile
solution.explanation: Write R = u² sin 2θ / g and H = u² sin²θ / (2g), set them equal and solve for tan θ.
steps: u² (2 sin θ cos θ)/g = u² sin²θ/(2g)
2 cos θ = sin θ / 2 → tan θ = 4
solution.shortcut: R = 4H cot θ for any projectile on level ground, so R = H gives tan θ = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: tan⁻¹(1/4) inverts the ratio. 45° is the angle for maximum range, not for R = H. tan⁻¹(2) uses H = u² sin²θ / g, dropping the 2 in the denominator.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body starts from rest and moves along a straight line with uniform acceleration. It covers 10 m during the third second of its motion. Its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Distance covered in the nth second
solution.explanation: The distance covered in the nth second is the distance in n seconds minus that in (n − 1) seconds: sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m/s² drops the factor ½ (uses sₙ = a(2n − 1)). 2.2 m/s² (= 20/9) treats 10 m as the distance in the first 3 s. 3.3 m/s² divides the distance by the time as if it were a velocity gained per second.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The magnitude of the resultant of two vectors can never exceed the sum of their magnitudes.
Reason (R): For two vectors of magnitudes A and B inclined at an angle θ, the resultant R satisfies R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ, and cos θ can never exceed 1.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Triangle (parallelogram) law of vector addition
solution.explanation: From R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ, the largest value of R occurs at cos θ = 1 (θ = 0), when R = A + B. For every other angle R < A + B. So the formula in R directly shows why A is true.
steps: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ ≤ A² + B² + 2AB = (A + B)²
So R ≤ A + B, with equality only for parallel vectors
A is true and R gives the reason → option A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and A follows directly from R, so B, C and D do not fit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', addition of vectors: analytical method
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A projectile is launched from level ground at 60° above the horizontal and lands back on the same level ground. Neglecting air resistance, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At the highest point, its speed is half its speed of projection.
(b) At the highest point, its acceleration is zero.
(c) At the highest point, its kinetic energy is one-fourth of its initial kinetic energy.
(d) The time taken to reach the highest point is half the total time of flight.
(e) Its horizontal range is the maximum possible for this speed of projection.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Velocity, acceleration and energy along a projectile's path
solution.explanation: At the top, only the horizontal velocity u cos θ remains; the acceleration is still g downward. For launch and landing at the same level the path is symmetric, so the rise takes half the flight time. Maximum range needs θ = 45°.
steps: (b) acceleration = g at every point → false
(e) range is maximum at 45°, not 60° → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (e) include a false statement; only (a), (c) and (d) are all true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is thrown from the top of a building 40 m high with a speed of 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the horizontal distance from the foot of the building at which the ball hits the level ground is:

solution.concept: Projectile launched from a height
solution.explanation: Find the time of flight from the vertical motion, taking upward as positive and the landing point 40 m below the launch point; then multiply by the constant horizontal velocity.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20√3 m uses the level-ground flight time of 2 s. 40 m uses the vertical component (u sin 30°) for the horizontal motion. 80 m multiplies the full speed by the time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A balloon is rising vertically with a constant speed of 5 m/s. When it is 30 m above the ground, a packet is released from it. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the time the packet takes to reach the ground is:

solution.concept: Free fall with an initial upward velocity
solution.explanation: At release the packet has the balloon's velocity, 5 m/s upward. With upward positive, its displacement on reaching the ground is −30 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: √6 s (≈ 2.45 s) ignores the packet's initial upward velocity. 2 s takes that velocity as downward. 1 s is only the time for the packet to rise and come back to the release point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two ships P and Q are on a calm sea. Initially Q is 80 m due north of P. P sails due east at 6 m/s and Q sails due south at 8 m/s, both with constant velocities. The minimum distance between the two ships is:

solution.concept: Relative velocity and closest approach
solution.explanation: In P's frame, Q moves in a straight line with the relative velocity v_QP = v_Q − v_P. The minimum separation is the perpendicular distance from P to this line.
steps: v_QP = (−6, −8) m/s → |v_QP| = 10 m/s; initial position of Q relative to P = (0, 80) m
Angle between the line PQ (north) and v_QP: sin α = 6/10 = 0.6
d_min = 80 × sin α = 80 × 0.6 = 48 m (reached at t = 6.4 s)
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 m assumes the ships collide, but their relative velocity does not point along PQ. 64 m uses cos α (0.8) instead of sin α. 80 m assumes the separation never decreases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', relative velocity in two dimensions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (motion) with List-II (description of its velocity and acceleration). Neglect air resistance.

List-I:
A. A particle in uniform circular motion
B. A ball projected at 30° above the horizontal, during its flight
C. A car moving with constant velocity on a straight road
D. A ball thrown vertically upward, at its highest point

List-II:
I. Zero acceleration with non-zero velocity
II. Zero velocity with non-zero acceleration
III. Acceleration of constant magnitude whose direction keeps changing
IV. Constant acceleration (in magnitude and direction) along a curved path

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Velocity and acceleration in different kinds of motion
solution.explanation: In uniform circular motion the acceleration v²/R always points to the centre, so its direction changes. A projectile has the constant acceleration g but a parabolic path. Uniform straight-line motion has no acceleration. At the top of a vertical throw the velocity is momentarily zero but the acceleration is still g.
steps: A: centripetal acceleration, constant magnitude, changing direction → III
B: acceleration g (constant), parabolic path → IV
C: constant velocity → zero acceleration → I
D: v = 0 at the top, a = g downward → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the circular and projectile motions (both curved), or assume that zero velocity at the top of a vertical throw means zero acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion and uniform circular motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 2 kg is at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 50 N acts on it for 0.2 s. The speed of the ball just after the force stops acting is:

solution.concept: Impulse–momentum theorem
solution.explanation: The impulse of a constant force, F Δt, equals the change in momentum of the body.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 m/s reports the impulse (in N s) as the speed, without dividing by the mass. 25 m/s is the acceleration F/m, not the speed. 20 m/s multiplies the impulse by the mass instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', impulse

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A book rests on a horizontal table. According to Newton's third law, the reaction to the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on the book is:

options.text: The normal force exerted by the table on the book
The force exerted by the book on the table
The force of friction exerted by the table on the book
The gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth

solution.concept: Action–reaction pairs
solution.explanation: An action–reaction pair consists of two forces of the same kind that two bodies exert on each other. The Earth pulls the book gravitationally, so the reaction is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth.
steps: Action: gravitational force of the Earth on the book
Reaction: gravitational force of the book on the Earth
The table's normal force also acts on the book, so it cannot be the reaction to a force on the book
solution.why_others_wrong: The normal force balances the weight, but it acts on the same body (the book), so it is not the third-law pair. The book's push on the table is the reaction to the normal force. There is no friction on a book resting on a horizontal table with no other horizontal force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's third law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: The gravitational force exerted by the book on the Earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 3 kg hangs from a light string tied to a fixed hook. A horizontal force F pulls the block aside, and it stays at rest with the string at 37° to the vertical. Taking g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6 and cos 37° = 0.8, F is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium of three concurrent forces
solution.explanation: Three forces act on the block: its weight mg, the tension T along the string and the horizontal force F. Resolving: T cos 37° = mg and T sin 37° = F, so F = mg tan 37°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 37.5 N is the tension, not F. 18 N uses mg sin 37°. 40 N uses mg cot 37°, mixing up the components.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 4 kg rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between them are 0.5 and 0.3. A horizontal force of 25 N is applied to the block. Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the block is:

solution.concept: Static and kinetic friction
solution.explanation: First check whether the block moves: the applied force must exceed the limiting static friction μₛN. Once it slides, kinetic friction μₖN opposes the motion.
steps: Limiting friction = 0.5 × 40 = 20 N < 25 N → the block slides
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.25 m/s² uses the static coefficient for a sliding block. 6.25 m/s² ignores friction. 0 assumes the block stays at rest, but 25 N exceeds the limiting friction of 20 N.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A man of mass 60 kg stands at rest in a boat of mass 120 kg floating at rest on still water. He jumps off horizontally with a velocity of 2 m/s relative to the ground. Neglecting water resistance, the speed with which the boat moves back is:

solution.concept: Conservation of linear momentum
solution.explanation: No external horizontal force acts on the man–boat system, so its total horizontal momentum stays zero.
steps: The boat moves back at 1 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m/s assumes equal speeds for unequal masses. 0.67 m/s adds the man's mass to the boat's after he has left it. 4 m/s inverts the mass ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A person of mass m stands on a weighing scale inside a lift. Match List-I (motion of the lift) with List-II (reading of the scale, in newtons). Here a is the magnitude of the lift's acceleration (a < g).

List-I:
A. Moving upward with constant velocity
B. Moving upward with increasing speed
C. Moving upward with decreasing speed
D. Falling freely after its cable breaks

List-II:
I. Zero
II. mg
III. m(g + a)
IV. m(g − a)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Apparent weight in an accelerating lift
solution.explanation: The scale reads the normal force N. From N − mg = m a_up, N = m(g + a_up). What matters is the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity.
steps: B: speeding up while going up → a upward → N = m(g + a) → III
C: slowing down while going up → a downward → N = m(g − a) → IV
D: free fall → a = g downward → N = 0 → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The commonest error is to give m(g + a) for any upward motion. A lift moving up but slowing down has a downward acceleration, so the reading falls below mg.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text: A car takes a turn of radius 45 m on a level (unbanked) road. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum speed at which the car can take the turn without skidding is:

solution.concept: Friction as the centripetal force on a level road
solution.explanation: On a level road, static friction alone provides the centripetal force: mv²/r ≤ μₛmg, so v_max = √(μₛrg).
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 km/h forgets to convert m/s to km/h. 108 km/h (30 m/s) divides by μₛ instead of multiplying. 76 km/h (≈ 21.2 m/s) leaves μₛ out altogether.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A block placed on a rough inclined plane remains at rest if the angle of inclination is less than the angle of repose θᵣ, where tan θᵣ = μₛ.
Statement II: For a block resting on a rough inclined plane whose angle of inclination θ is less than the angle of repose, the static friction acting on the block is mg sin θ, up the plane.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Angle of repose and self-adjusting static friction
solution.explanation: The block is on the verge of sliding when mg sin θ = μₛ mg cos θ, i.e. tan θ = μₛ. Below this angle the block stays at rest, and static friction adjusts itself to exactly balance the component of gravity along the plane.
steps: Statement I: block slips only when tan θ exceeds μₛ → true
Statement II: at rest, net force along the plane is zero → f = mg sin θ (less than μₛmg cos θ) → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is not the limiting friction μₛmg cos θ: static friction equals mg sin θ, which is smaller than the limiting value when θ < θᵣ. Both statements are true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A cricketer moves his hands backward while catching a fast-moving ball.
Reason (R): Moving the hands back increases the time over which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero, so the average force exerted on the hands is smaller.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Impulse: F_avg = Δp/Δt
solution.explanation: The change in momentum of the ball is fixed by its mass and speed. Spreading that change over a longer time reduces the average force, which is exactly why the cricketer draws his hands back.
steps: F_avg = Δp/Δt; larger Δt → smaller F_avg
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is the reason for A, so B, C and D do not fit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', impulse
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg lies on a rough horizontal table (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.25). It is tied to a light inextensible string that passes over a smooth, light pulley at the edge of the table and carries a hanging block of mass 3 kg. When the system moves, the tension in the string is (g = 10 m/s²):

solution.concept: Connected bodies with friction
solution.explanation: Write Newton's second law for each block. For the hanging block: 3g − T = 3a. For the block on the table: T − μₖ(2g) = 2a.
steps: Check with the hanging block: T = 30 − 3 × 5 = 15 N ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 N writes T = 2a for the table block and forgets the friction it must also overcome. 12 N ignores friction altogether (a = 6 m/s²). 30 N takes the tension equal to the hanging weight, which holds only when nothing accelerates.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', solving problems in mechanics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text: A circular track of radius 20 m is banked at an angle θ with tan θ = 0.75. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the track is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum speed at which a car can go round the track without skidding is:

solution.concept: Banked road with friction
solution.explanation: At the maximum speed, friction acts down the slope. Resolving forces vertically and horizontally gives v²_max = rg(μₛ + tan θ)/(1 − μₛ tan θ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.2 m/s is the optimum (friction-free) speed √(rg tan θ). 13.5 m/s puts + instead of − in the denominator. 15.8 m/s leaves out the denominator.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', circular motion (motion of a car on a banked road)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block A of mass 2 kg rests on top of a block B of mass 4 kg, which lies on a frictionless horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between A and B is 0.3. A horizontal force F is applied to the lower block B. Taking g = 10 m/s², the largest value of F for which the two blocks move together without slipping is:

solution.concept: Friction as the only force accelerating the upper block
solution.explanation: Only static friction from B accelerates A, so A's acceleration cannot exceed μₛg. The two blocks move together at that acceleration under the largest force.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 N is the limiting friction μₛm_A g itself, not the applied force. 12 N uses the mass of B in the friction force. 9 N is the answer when F is applied to the upper block A instead of B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If the net external force on a body is zero, the body must be at rest.
(b) Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they do not cancel each other.
(c) The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum it produces.
(d) A body moving in a circle with constant speed has a constant linear momentum.
(e) The mass of a body is a quantitative measure of its inertia.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Newton's laws of motion
solution.explanation: Zero net force means zero acceleration, which allows uniform motion as well as rest. Momentum is a vector, so it changes when the direction of motion changes even at constant speed.
steps: (a) False: the body may move with constant velocity
(b) True: the pair acts on two different bodies
(d) False: the direction of the velocity, and hence of the momentum, keeps changing
(e) True: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (a) or (d) include a false statement; the option without (c) leaves out a true one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's laws of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A constant force of 10 N acts on a body, making an angle of 60° with the direction of its displacement. The body is displaced through 5 m. The work done by the force is:

solution.concept: Work done by a constant force: W = F d cos θ
solution.explanation: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work.
steps: W = F d cos θ = 10 × 5 × cos 60°
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 J ignores the angle. 25√3 J uses sin 60° in place of cos 60°. −25 J has the wrong sign: for an angle below 90° the work is positive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (expression).

List-I:
A. Work done by a variable force F(x) as a body moves from x₁ to x₂
B. Kinetic energy of a body of mass m and linear momentum p
C. Instantaneous power delivered by a force F to a body moving with velocity v
D. Potential energy of a spring of spring constant k stretched by x

List-II:
I. ½kx²
II. F · v
III. p²/2m
IV. ∫ F dx, taken from x₁ to x₂

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Work, kinetic energy, power and spring potential energy
solution.explanation: Work by a variable force is the area under the F–x curve. Writing K = ½mv² with v = p/m gives p²/2m. Power is the rate of doing work, dW/dt = F · v. A spring stretched by x stores ½kx².
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap power with work, or kinetic energy with the spring's potential energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work by a variable force, power, potential energy of a spring
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The kinetic energy of a moving body remains constant over a certain time interval. Which of the following must be true over that interval?

options.text: No force acts on the body
The net work done on the body is zero
The body moves in a straight line
The linear momentum of the body remains constant

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem
solution.explanation: The work–energy theorem states that the work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy. If the kinetic energy does not change, the net work is zero. Forces may still act, and the direction of motion may change.
steps: Example: uniform circular motion has constant K but a net (centripetal) force
In that example the path is curved and the momentum changes direction
solution.why_others_wrong: A body in uniform circular motion keeps a constant kinetic energy although a net force acts on it, its path is not straight and its momentum keeps changing direction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work-energy theorem
solution.final_answer: Option B: The net work done on the body is zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg slides on a rough horizontal floor with an initial speed of 10 m/s. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Taking g = 10 m/s², the distance it slides before coming to rest is:

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem with friction
solution.explanation: Friction is the only force doing work. The work it does, −μₖmg d, equals the change in kinetic energy, −½mv². The mass cancels.
steps: μₖ m g d = ½ m v²
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 m drops the ½ in the kinetic energy. 10 m divides once more by the mass (2 kg), which actually cancels. 4 m is the stopping time (v/μₖg = 4 s) taken as a distance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work-energy theorem

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 0.5 kg moving at 2 m/s on a smooth horizontal surface hits the free end of a light horizontal spring of spring constant 200 N/m, whose other end is fixed. The maximum compression of the spring is:

solution.concept: Conservation of mechanical energy with a spring
solution.explanation: At maximum compression the block is momentarily at rest, so all its kinetic energy has become elastic potential energy of the spring.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.1 cm writes the spring energy as kx² (drops the ½ on one side only). 1 cm forgets the square root (x² = 0.01 taken as x). 0.5 cm equates kx to the momentum mv.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a perfectly inelastic collision, the total kinetic energy of the colliding bodies always becomes zero.
Reason (R): In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies stick together and move with a common velocity after the collision.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Perfectly inelastic collisions
solution.explanation: The bodies stick together, so they share a common final velocity. Momentum is conserved, so if the total momentum before the collision is not zero, the combined body must keep moving and some kinetic energy remains. The kinetic energy becomes zero only in the special case of zero total momentum.
steps: R: bodies move together after the collision → true
A: e.g. a moving body sticking to an identical body at rest keeps half the kinetic energy → false
A false, R true → option D
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because 'always' ignores momentum conservation, which forces the combined body to move whenever the total momentum is non-zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A stone tied to a string and whirled in a vertical circle, moving under gravity and the tension of the string only, moves with constant speed.
Statement II: For a stone tied to a string and whirled in a vertical circle, the tension in the string is maximum at the lowest point.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Motion in a vertical circle
solution.explanation: Gravity does work on the stone as it rises and falls, so its speed is greatest at the bottom and least at the top. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/L, so T = mg + mv²/L, which is the largest tension anywhere on the circle.
steps: Statement I: kinetic energy changes with height → speed is not constant → false
Statement II: speed is maximum and the weight acts directly away from the centre at the bottom → T is maximum there → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I would hold only for uniform motion in a horizontal circle. In a vertical circle the speed changes with height.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two bodies of equal mass, moving with equal speeds along perpendicular directions on a smooth horizontal surface, collide and stick together. The fraction of their total initial kinetic energy that is lost in the collision is:

solution.concept: Perfectly inelastic collision in two dimensions
solution.explanation: Momentum is a vector. The two equal perpendicular momenta add to a resultant √2 mv, carried by mass 2m.
steps: Final momentum = √2 mv → final speed = √2 mv/(2m) = v/√2
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/4 takes the final speed as v/2 (one body's momentum shared by 2m). 0 adds the momenta as scalars, as if the bodies moved in the same direction. 1 assumes the bodies stop, which happens only for equal and opposite momenta.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions in two dimensions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small stone of mass 0.5 kg is whirled in a vertical circle at the end of a light string 1 m long. Its speed is such that the tension in the string just becomes zero at the highest point. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string at the lowest point is:

solution.concept: Vertical circle: critical speed and tension
solution.explanation: Zero tension at the top means mg alone provides the centripetal force there: v_top² = gL. Energy conservation gives the speed at the bottom, and the radial equation there gives the tension.
steps: T_bottom = mg + m v_bottom²/L = mg + 5mg = 6mg = 6 × 5 = 30 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 N (5mg) forgets that the tension must also balance the weight at the bottom. 5 N is just the weight. 15 N (3mg) takes the speed at the top as zero, which is possible only for a rod, not a string.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a level road with its engine delivering a constant power of 20 kW. The total resistance to its motion is a constant 1000 N. At the instant its speed is 10 m/s, its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Power and force: P = F v
solution.explanation: At constant power the engine's driving force depends on speed: F = P/v. The net force is this driving force minus the resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m/s² ignores the resistance. 3 m/s² adds the resistance to the driving force. 20 m/s² divides the power by the mass, which is not a force at all.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A force F = 4î N acts at a point whose position vector relative to the origin is r = (2î + 3ĵ) m. The torque of the force about the origin is:

solution.concept: Torque as a vector product: τ = r × F
solution.explanation: Use î × î = 0 and ĵ × î = −k̂, keeping the order r × F.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12k̂ N m takes F × r, reversing the order. 8k̂ N m multiplies the x-components, which give zero in a cross product. −12î N m has the right magnitude but a direction that is not perpendicular to both r and F.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of force (torque)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its dimensional formula).

List-I:
A. Torque
B. Angular momentum
C. Moment of inertia
D. Angular acceleration

List-II:
I. [M L² T⁻¹]
II. [T⁻²]
III. [M L² T⁻²]
IV. [M L²]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensions of rotational quantities
solution.explanation: Torque = force × distance; angular momentum = moment of inertia × angular velocity; moment of inertia = mass × (distance)²; angular acceleration = angular velocity per unit time, and angle is dimensionless.
steps: Torque: [M L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²] → III
Angular momentum: [M L²][T⁻¹] = [M L² T⁻¹] → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap torque with angular momentum (they differ by one power of T), or moment of inertia with angular acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', torque, angular momentum, moment of inertia
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: The radius of gyration of a uniform circular disc of radius 20 cm, about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane, is:

solution.concept: Radius of gyration: I = Mk²
solution.explanation: For a uniform disc about its central perpendicular axis, I = MR²/2. Equating this to Mk² gives k = R/√2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm is the result for a thin ring (I = MR²). 10 cm takes k = R/2. 4√10 cm uses the solid-sphere result I = 2MR²/5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina lies at:

options.text: The orthocentre, the point where its three altitudes meet
The midpoint of its longest side
The centroid, the point where its three medians meet
The vertex opposite its longest side

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a uniform lamina from symmetry
solution.explanation: Divide the lamina into thin strips parallel to one side. The centre of mass of each strip is at its midpoint, and these midpoints lie on the median to that side. So the centre of mass lies on every median, i.e. at the centroid.
steps: Strips parallel to BC have midpoints on the median from A
The same holds for the other two medians
Centre of mass = intersection of the medians (centroid)
solution.why_others_wrong: The orthocentre coincides with the centroid only for an equilateral triangle. A side's midpoint and a vertex lie on the boundary, not at the balance point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass
solution.final_answer: Option C: The centroid, the point where its three medians meet

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ice skater spins about a vertical axis at 2 revolutions per second with her arms stretched out, when her moment of inertia is 6 kg m². She pulls her arms in, reducing her moment of inertia to 4 kg m². Neglecting friction, her new rate of spin is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum
solution.explanation: With no external torque about the vertical axis, angular momentum Iω is conserved. Kinetic energy is not conserved: she does work pulling her arms in.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.33 rev/s inverts the ratio of moments of inertia. 2.45 rev/s wrongly conserves rotational kinetic energy (I₁ω₁² = I₂ω₂²). 2 rev/s assumes the rate of spin does not change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Particles of masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are placed at the points (0, 0), (3 m, 0) and (0, 3 m) of the x–y plane. The coordinates of their centre of mass are:

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a system of particles
solution.explanation: Each coordinate of the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average of that coordinate: X = Σmᵢxᵢ/M, Y = Σmᵢyᵢ/M.
solution.why_others_wrong: (1.5 m, 1 m) swaps the coordinates. (1 m, 1 m) is the simple (unweighted) average of the positions. (2 m, 3 m) divides by the number of particles (3) instead of the total mass (6 kg).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin circular ring has mass 2 kg and radius 10 cm. Its moment of inertia about a tangent to the ring lying in the plane of the ring is:

solution.concept: Perpendicular and parallel axis theorems
solution.explanation: First find the moment of inertia about a diameter with the perpendicular axis theorem (two equal diameters add up to the central perpendicular axis). Then shift to the parallel tangent in the plane with the parallel axis theorem.
steps: I(central perpendicular axis) = MR² = 0.02 kg m²
I(tangent in plane) = MR²/2 + MR² = 3MR²/2 = 1.5 × 2 × 0.01 = 0.03 kg m²
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.04 kg m² (2MR²) is for a tangent perpendicular to the plane. 0.01 kg m² is about a diameter. 0.02 kg m² is about the central axis perpendicular to the plane.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The handle of a door is fixed near the edge farthest from the hinges.
Reason (R): For a force of given magnitude applied perpendicular to the door, the torque about the hinge line is proportional to the distance of the point of application from the hinge line.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Torque = force × perpendicular distance
solution.explanation: To turn the door we need a certain torque about the hinges. Since τ = F r⊥, putting the handle as far as possible from the hinges lets the smallest force produce that torque.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is exactly why the handle is placed far from the hinges.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of force (torque)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about an axis does not depend on how its mass is distributed about that axis.
Statement II: The radius of gyration of a rigid body has the same value about every axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Moment of inertia and radius of gyration
solution.explanation: I = Σmᵢrᵢ² depends on the mass and on how far each part is from the axis, i.e. on the distribution of mass about the axis. Since k = √(I/M), the radius of gyration changes whenever I changes from one axis to another.
steps: Statement I: a ring and a disc of equal mass and radius have different I → false
Statement II: e.g. a rod has k = L/√12 about its centre and L/√3 about one end → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements contradict the definition I = Σmr², so 'both false' is the only consistent choice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A light string is wound round a uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 10 cm that can rotate freely about a fixed horizontal axis through its centre. A block of mass 1 kg hangs from the free end of the string. Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the block when it is released is:

solution.concept: Coupled translation and rotation: τ = Iα with a = Rα
solution.explanation: For the block: mg − T = ma. For the disc: TR = Iα = (MR²/2)(a/R), so T = Ma/2. Adding eliminates T.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 m/s² takes T = mg (the block's weight drives the disc as if the block were not accelerating). 3.3 m/s² uses I = MR² (a ring). 6.7 m/s² uses I = MR²/4 (the disc about a diameter).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform plank 6 m long and of mass 30 kg rests horizontally on two supports, each 1.5 m from an end. A man of mass 60 kg walks along the plank from its centre towards one end. The greatest distance from the centre he can walk before the plank starts to tip is:

solution.concept: Rotational equilibrium and tipping
solution.explanation: When the man passes a support, the plank is on the point of tipping about that support once the reaction at the other support becomes zero. Then the torques of the man's weight and the plank's weight about the near support balance.
steps: The plank's centre of mass is 1.5 m from each support
At tipping: 60g × d = 30g × 1.5 → d = 0.75 m beyond the support
Distance from centre = 1.5 + 0.75 = 2.25 m (less than the 3 m to the end)
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.75 m is the distance beyond the support, not from the centre. 1.5 m stops at the support, where nothing tips. 3.0 m is the end of the plank; it tips before he reaches it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A horizontal platform with a moment of inertia of 300 kg m² about its vertical axis rotates freely at 2 rad/s. A man of mass 50 kg, standing at the axis, walks out radially to a point 2 m from the axis. Treating the man as a point mass and neglecting friction, the new angular speed of the platform is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum with a changing moment of inertia
solution.explanation: No external torque acts about the vertical axis. At the axis the man adds nothing to the moment of inertia; at 2 m he adds mr².
steps: I₁ = 300 kg m² (man at the axis)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 rad/s ignores the change in moment of inertia. 0.8 rad/s uses the man's share (200/500) instead of the platform's. 3.3 rad/s inverts the ratio of moments of inertia.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If the net external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum is conserved.
(b) A rigid body on which the net external force is zero must also be in rotational equilibrium.
(c) Of all axes parallel to a given direction, the moment of inertia of a body is least about the axis through its centre of mass.
(d) For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the torque about that axis equals the moment of inertia about the axis times the angular acceleration.
(e) The rotational kinetic energy of a body spinning with a given angular speed is the same about every axis.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Torque, angular momentum and moment of inertia
solution.explanation: dL/dt = τ_ext, so zero external torque keeps L constant. A couple gives zero net force but a non-zero torque. By the parallel axis theorem I = I_cm + Md², which is least when d = 0. Rotational kinetic energy ½Iω² depends on I, which depends on the axis.
steps: (b) False: a couple gives F_net = 0 but τ ≠ 0
(d) True: τ = Iα about a fixed axis
(e) False: I, and so ½Iω², changes with the axis
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (e) include a false statement; (a), (c) and (d) are all true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body, moment of inertia, angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two uniform solid spheres, each of mass 100 kg and radius 0.1 m, are placed so that the gap between their surfaces is 0.3 m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the gravitational force between them is about:

solution.concept: Newton's law of gravitation for uniform spheres
solution.explanation: A uniform sphere attracts an outside mass as if all its mass were at its centre, so r is the distance between the centres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.41 × 10⁻⁶ N uses the 0.3 m gap between the surfaces instead of the distance between centres. 1.33 × 10⁻⁶ N divides by r instead of r². 2.67 × 10⁻⁸ N uses only one of the masses.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Kepler's second law (the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time) follows from the conservation of the planet's:

solution.concept: Kepler's law of areas and central forces
solution.explanation: The gravitational force on the planet is directed towards the Sun (a central force), so it exerts no torque about the Sun. The planet's angular momentum L about the Sun is therefore constant, and the areal velocity dA/dt = L/2m is constant.
steps: Central force → τ about the Sun = 0 → L constant
dA/dt = L/(2m) = constant → equal areas in equal times
solution.why_others_wrong: The planet's linear momentum, kinetic energy and speed all change along an elliptical orbit: it moves fastest near the Sun.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', Kepler's laws
solution.final_answer: Option D: Angular momentum about the Sun

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The acceleration due to gravity at a small height h above the Earth's surface is 1% less than its value at the surface. Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km, h is about:

solution.concept: Variation of g with height (h ≪ R)
solution.explanation: For h much smaller than R, g(h) ≈ g(1 − 2h/R), so the fractional decrease in g is 2h/R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 km uses the depth formula g(1 − d/R), which has no factor 2. 16 km uses a factor 4 instead of 2. 320 km takes 1% as 0.1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below and above the surface of the Earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (location) with List-II (acceleration due to gravity there). The Earth is a uniform sphere of radius R, g is the value at its surface and its rotation is ignored.

List-I:
A. At a small height h above the surface (h ≪ R)
B. At a depth d below the surface
C. At the centre of the Earth
D. At a height equal to R above the surface

List-II:
I. Zero
II. g/4
III. g(1 − d/R)
IV. g(1 − 2h/R)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Variation of g with height and depth
solution.explanation: Above the surface g = gR²/(R + h)², which is g(1 − 2h/R) for small h and g/4 at h = R. Inside a uniform Earth, only the mass within radius (R − d) attracts, giving g(1 − d/R), which is zero at the centre.
solution.why_others_wrong: The commonest swap is between the height and depth formulas (factor 2h/R versus d/R). At h = R the small-height formula does not apply; the exact result is g/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below and above the surface of the Earth
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite revolves in a circular orbit just above the Earth's surface with orbital speed v₀. Neglecting air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the minimum additional speed it must be given along its direction of motion so that it escapes the Earth's gravity is:

solution.concept: Orbital speed and escape speed near the surface
solution.explanation: Near the surface, the orbital speed is v₀ = √(gR) and the escape speed is vₑ = √(2gR) = √2 v₀. The satellite already moves at v₀, so it needs only the difference.
solution.why_others_wrong: √2 v₀ is the full escape speed, not the extra speed. v₀ assumes the escape speed is twice the orbital speed. (√2 + 1)v₀ adds the two speeds instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', escape speed and earth satellites

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the zero of gravitational potential energy is taken at infinite separation, the gravitational potential energy of a system of two particles is negative.
Reason (R): The universal gravitational constant G has the same value for all pairs of bodies everywhere in the universe.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Gravitational potential energy and the universality of G
solution.explanation: U = −Gm₁m₂/r. The negative sign arises because gravity is attractive: the energy rises to zero as the particles are pulled apart to infinity, so at any finite separation it is below zero. R is a true statement about G being a universal constant, but it says nothing about why U is negative.
steps: A: U = −Gm₁m₂/r < 0 for finite r → true
R: G is a universal constant → true
The sign of U comes from the attractive nature of gravity, not from the universality of G → option B
solution.why_others_wrong: R does not explain A: U would be negative even if G varied from place to place, because the sign comes from gravity being attractive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The escape speed of a body from the Earth's surface depends on the mass of the body.
Statement II: Neglecting air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the escape speed from the Earth's surface does not depend on the direction in which the body is projected.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Escape speed
solution.explanation: Escape requires ½mvₑ² − GMm/R ≥ 0, so vₑ = √(2GM/R). The mass m of the body cancels, and the energy condition involves only the speed, not the direction.
steps: Statement I: m cancels in the energy condition → false
Statement II: kinetic energy is a scalar → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false because both the kinetic energy needed and the potential energy to overcome are proportional to m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', escape speed
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite of mass 200 kg revolves in a circular orbit at a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius. Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km and g at the surface as 10 m/s², the total mechanical energy of the satellite is:

solution.concept: Energy of a satellite in a circular orbit
solution.explanation: For a circular orbit of radius r, the kinetic energy is GMm/2r, the potential energy is −GMm/r, and the total energy is −GMm/2r. Use GM = gR².
solution.why_others_wrong: −6.4 × 10⁹ J is the potential energy in this orbit (or the total energy with r taken as R). +3.2 × 10⁹ J is the kinetic energy. −1.28 × 10¹⁰ J is −mgR, the potential energy at the Earth's surface.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mass of the Earth is 81 times that of the Moon, and the distance between their centres is d. The point on the line joining their centres where the net gravitational field due to the two bodies is zero is at a distance from the Earth's centre of:

solution.concept: Neutral point between two masses
solution.explanation: At the neutral point the fields of the Earth and the Moon are equal and opposite: GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)².
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1d is the distance from the Moon, not the Earth. 81d/82 and d/82 use the mass ratio 81 directly, forgetting to take the square root.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a satellite revolving round the Earth in a circular orbit, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its orbital speed does not depend on its own mass.
(b) Its kinetic energy is equal to the magnitude of its total mechanical energy.
(c) Its total mechanical energy is positive.
(d) Its orbital speed increases as the radius of the orbit increases.
(e) Its gravitational potential energy is twice its total mechanical energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Speed and energy of an orbiting satellite
solution.explanation: From GMm/r² = mv²/r, v = √(GM/r), which does not involve m and falls as r grows. K = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r and E = K + U = −GMm/2r. So K = |E| and U = 2E, and E is negative for a bound orbit.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (d) include a false statement; (a), (b) and (e) are all true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites and energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire of cross-sectional area 2 mm² is stretched by a force of 100 N applied along its length. The tensile stress in the wire is:

solution.concept: Stress = force / area
solution.explanation: Convert the area to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²) before dividing.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 N m⁻² leaves the area in mm². 5 × 10⁵ N m⁻² takes 1 mm² as 10⁻⁴ m² (that is 1 cm²). 2 × 10⁻⁸ N m⁻² divides the area by the force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', stress and strain

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the atmospheric pressure as 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the density of water as 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s², the absolute pressure at a depth of 20 m below the surface of a lake is:

solution.concept: Pressure at a depth in a liquid
solution.explanation: The absolute pressure at depth h is the atmospheric pressure on the surface plus the pressure of the liquid column: P = Pₐ + ρgh.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa is the gauge pressure, leaving out the atmosphere. 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa uses ρh without g. 2.0 × 10⁴ Pa is ρh alone, with neither g nor the atmospheric pressure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', variation of pressure with depth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water has its maximum density at:

solution.concept: Anomalous expansion of water
solution.explanation: Water contracts on heating from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands above 4 °C, so its volume is least and its density greatest at 4 °C.
steps: Minimum volume, hence maximum density, at 4 °C
solution.why_others_wrong: At 0 °C water is less dense than at 4 °C (which is why lakes freeze from the top). 100 °C is the boiling point at 1 atm, and −4 °C is below the normal freezing point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: As the temperature of a black body is raised, the wavelength at which it emits the maximum energy:

solution.concept: Wien's displacement law
solution.explanation: Wien's displacement law states λ_m T = constant, so λ_m is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature.
steps: T increases → λ_m decreases (e.g. a heated iron piece glows dull red, then orange, then yellowish white)
solution.why_others_wrong: λ_m T is constant, so λ_m cannot increase or stay the same when T rises, and the change is monotonic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', radiation (Wien's displacement law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Water is used as the coolant in the radiators of automobiles.
Reason (R): Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs a large amount of heat for a small rise in its temperature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Specific heat capacity of water
solution.explanation: A coolant must carry away a lot of heat from the engine without itself getting too hot. Because water's specific heat capacity is high, Q = mcΔT is large for a small ΔT, which is exactly why it is used.
steps: Q = mcΔT; large c → large Q for small ΔT
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R gives the property that makes water a good coolant.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A clean glass capillary tube of internal diameter 0.2 mm is dipped vertically in water. The surface tension of water is 0.07 N/m, the angle of contact is 0°, the density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s². The height to which water rises in the tube is:

solution.concept: Capillary rise: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr)
solution.explanation: The upward pull of surface tension round the circumference balances the weight of the raised column. Use the radius, which is half the given diameter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 cm puts the diameter in place of the radius. 28 cm uses 4S, the factor for a soap bubble with two surfaces. 1.4 cm is a power-of-ten slip in converting metres to centimetres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', capillary rise

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small steel ball of radius 1 mm and density 8000 kg/m³ falls through a liquid of density 800 kg/m³ and coefficient of viscosity 0.8 Pa s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and assuming Stokes' law holds, its terminal velocity is:

solution.concept: Terminal velocity from Stokes' law
solution.explanation: At terminal velocity, weight = buoyant force + viscous drag, which gives v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.2 cm/s ignores the buoyant force (uses ρ instead of ρ − σ). 1 cm/s drops the factor 2. 8 cm/s uses the diameter (2 mm) as the radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity and Stokes' law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows steadily at 2 m/s through a horizontal hose pipe of internal radius 1 cm. At its end is a nozzle of internal radius 0.5 cm, pointed vertically upward. Neglecting viscosity and air resistance, and taking g = 10 m/s², the height above the nozzle to which the jet rises is:

solution.concept: Equation of continuity and conservation of energy
solution.explanation: The volume flow rate Av is the same in the pipe and the nozzle, so the speed rises as the area falls. The jet then rises until its kinetic energy is used up: h = v²/2g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.8 m uses the ratio of radii instead of areas (v₂ = 4 m/s). 6.4 m drops the 2 in v²/2g. 0.2 m uses the speed in the pipe, not in the nozzle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', streamline flow and Bernoulli's principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Gases have much smaller bulk moduli than solids.
Statement II: For most materials, the shear modulus is greater than Young's modulus.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Bulk modulus and shear modulus
solution.explanation: Gases are far more compressible than solids, so their bulk moduli (B = −p/(ΔV/V)) are much smaller. NCERT notes that the shear modulus is generally less than Young's modulus; for most materials G ≈ Y/3.
steps: Statement I: gases are highly compressible → small B → true
Statement II: G is generally less than Y (about Y/3) → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the usual order: the shear modulus is generally smaller than Young's modulus.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', shear modulus and bulk modulus
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Small drops of a liquid take a nearly spherical shape.
Reason (R): Surface tension makes a liquid surface tend to have the least possible area, and for a given volume a sphere has the least surface area.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Surface tension and minimum surface area
solution.explanation: Surface energy is proportional to surface area, so a free liquid surface tends to contract to the least area. For small drops, surface effects dominate over gravity, and the shape with least area for a given volume is a sphere.
steps: Least area for a given volume → sphere
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is the reason small drops are spherical.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (elastic constant) with List-II (its definition).

List-I:
A. Young's modulus
B. Bulk modulus
C. Shear modulus (modulus of rigidity)
D. Compressibility

List-II:
I. Shearing (tangential) stress divided by shearing strain
II. Reciprocal of the bulk modulus
III. Tensile (or compressive) stress divided by longitudinal strain
IV. Hydraulic pressure divided by the magnitude of the volume strain

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Elastic moduli
solution.explanation: Each modulus is a stress divided by the matching strain: longitudinal for Young's modulus, volume for the bulk modulus and shearing for the shear modulus. Compressibility k is defined as 1/B.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap Young's modulus with the shear modulus, or the bulk modulus with its reciprocal (compressibility).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', elastic moduli
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two wires P and Q are made of the same material. The length of P is twice that of Q, and the diameter of P is half that of Q. When the same load is hung from each, the ratio of the extension of P to that of Q is:

solution.concept: Extension from Young's modulus: ΔL = FL/(AY)
solution.explanation: With the same load and material, ΔL ∝ L/A and A ∝ d².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 8 inverts the ratio. 4 : 1 uses the diameter instead of its square. 1 : 2 multiplies by the area ratio instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steel rod of cross-sectional area 1 cm² is held between two rigid walls so that it cannot expand. Its temperature is raised by 50 °C. For steel, the coefficient of linear expansion is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ °C⁻¹ and Young's modulus is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m². The force the rod exerts on each wall is:

solution.concept: Thermal stress
solution.explanation: If free, the rod would expand by a strain αΔT. The walls prevent this, so they compress it by the same strain, which needs a stress YαΔT. The force is this stress times the area.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 × 10⁸ N is the stress (in N/m²) quoted as a force. 1.2 × 10⁶ N takes 1 cm² as 10⁻² m². 1.2 × 10² N takes 1 cm² as 10⁻⁶ m².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body cools from 80 °C to 60 °C in 5 minutes in a room at 20 °C. Using Newton's law of cooling in its approximate form (rate of fall of temperature = K × (average temperature of the body during the interval − room temperature)), the time it takes to cool further from 60 °C to 40 °C is:

solution.concept: Newton's law of cooling (average-temperature form)
solution.explanation: Apply the law to each interval with the average temperature of the body. The first interval gives K; the second then gives the time.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 min assumes equal drops take equal times, but the body cools more slowly as it nears room temperature. 7.5 min uses the starting temperatures (80 °C and 60 °C) instead of the averages. 7 min uses the averages but forgets to subtract the room temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', Newton's law of cooling

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A soap bubble of radius 1 cm is blown slowly (at constant temperature) from a soap solution of surface tension 0.03 N/m. The work done in blowing it is:

solution.concept: Surface energy of a film with two surfaces
solution.explanation: Work done at constant temperature = surface tension × increase in surface area. A soap bubble is a thin film with an inner and an outer surface, so the new area is 2 × 4πr².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2π × 10⁻⁵ J counts only one surface, as for a liquid drop. 0.6π × 10⁻⁵ J uses πr² for the area of each surface. 0.24π J leaves r in centimetres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension and surface energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a liquid at rest in an open container, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At any point in the liquid, the pressure is the same in all directions.
(b) The pressure is the same at all points at the same horizontal level in the liquid.
(c) The pressure at a given depth depends on the shape of the container.
(d) The gauge pressure at a point is the absolute pressure there minus the atmospheric pressure.
(e) Pressure is a vector quantity, because it acts in all directions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Pressure in a fluid at rest
